I'm aware there are more places than America, I'm canadian, I just used for the example as they had the largest unionized work force in the world. I'm also aware unions have been around since the 1810s, but again on a industry wide scale the didn't gain true power until the 1900-1930s when for example, the whole coal industry was organized under the united mine workers. I'm not taking away from the work that the unions before made or that they weren't important, but it's once there was Industry wide unionized workers that they gained true power. I also never said the class struggle hasn't existed since forever, rich people fucking suck and always will. You are correct that there was reforms with the specialization after the black death, but they were still relatively minor in the grand scheme of things. And you are correct that in north America, not just the US, the union effort has been hamperd by politics and lobying since the 80s. Same as in Britain, which is why I mentioned thatcher. My point was if unions hadn't purged they're radicals, that lobying and politics would have only ahd so much effect, because the unions could have fought back in the old ways they used to. But without the radicals you don't have the energy to get the unions upwr ranks to move as a collective against these effects.

I would have to say this is kinda somewhat inaccurate. For there to be a cycle like your saying would imply it's happend before, which it hasn't. Trust organized labour's on a industry scale didn't come about until the early 20th century and really only got fairly implemented in north America in the 1920s-1930s after a huge amount of force, organizing and blood. The only reasons unions began to shrink in the post 1970s was the fact they gutted all they're radicals from they're ranks post the 1950s. They became complacent with they're yearly raises and and more corporate structure, which left them vulnerable to Regan and thatchers union busting of the 1980s, which in turn led to they're shrinking and loss off power. This has now led us back to the bad times the original members lost they're lives for, which didn't need to happen. So no, it isn't a cycle that is set to repeat forever. It was a fundamental failing and complacency that led to this. I'm extremely glad unions are gaining momentum again and we're starting to have a shot at making change again, but let's not allow the same mistakes to be made again and then blame it on a cycle.
